on_yellow_card_wall.blurb: A compact wall within The Swamp, a south-facing cliff in the Beaver Valley uplands, with a dozen routes and a lean toward sport leads. Ten are bolted and two are trad, including a moderate crack line that is the wall's best-known climb. The wall takes its name from the yellow lichen across its face. Grades start easy but most of the climbing sits in the 5.12 range, with a handful of 5.9 to 5.11 lines mixed in, so it suits steady leaders looking for hard moves more than first-time cragging. Tree cover and shaded crevices keep parts of the cliff cool, and the area as a whole is regarded as a good choice in spring and fall.

on_the_last_stand_wall.blurb: The final big sector to be developed at The Swamp, a south-facing cliff in the Beaver Valley country of southern Ontario. It holds twelve routes, nine of them bolted and three on trad gear. The range is wide: a few easy and moderate lines in the 5.6 to 5.9 bracket, one 5.10, and a stronger cluster at 5.11 and 5.12 that includes some of the best-rated hard sport climbs on the cliff. A well-liked 5.10 trad line is the standout for gear climbers. Heavy tree cover and shaded crevices temper the southern exposure, and the cliff works well in cooler spring and fall weather. Grades there are said to run a little soft.

on_bethel_lake.blurb: A small, convenient sport crag on the edge of Sudbury, reached from South Bay Road near Laurentian University. Twelve routes, eleven of them bolted and one set up for top-roping, run roughly 8 to 15 metres, so the climbs are short rather than sustained. Most grades fall between 5.10 and 5.11, with a couple of 5.9s and a lone 5.8, so it favours climbers already comfortable on steeper bolted lines; the two best-rated routes are both 5.11a. The walk in is very short on a worn trail, which makes it popular for a quick after-work session. The Sudbury area has many other crags if you want to link several.

on_black_forest_wall.blurb: The trad-leaning side of Old Baldy, a popular Beaver Valley cliff near Kimberley. Eleven routes mix six on gear with five bolted lines, and the climbing feels different from the mostly sport-bolted rest of the cliff. Expect one easy scramble-grade line, a 5.9, a pair of 5.10s, and then a stronger run at 5.11 and 5.12, with a well-rated 5.12a among them. The Black Forest offers a welcome break from the strong afternoon sun that bakes much of Old Baldy, so it can be a pleasant pick on a warm day. Leading ability is needed, since the cliff is not set up for top-roping.

on_9k_lost_at_sea_wall.blurb: A steep, advanced sport wall at Lion's Head on the Bruce Peninsula, above Georgian Bay. Eleven bolted routes are gathered around a ledge, and many are done by working down to the climb from above and then climbing out. Grades begin around 5.10 and climb steeply from there: a few at 5.10 and 5.11, a larger group at 5.12 and 5.13, and a single 5.14. This is not a place for beginners or for a first outing with rope skills still developing; the area as a whole demands more technical experience than typical cragging. The approach is a long hike along the Bruce Trail to the cliff top.
on_9k_lost_at_sea_wall.approach: From the Bruce Trail parking, follow the white-blazed trail roughly two miles to the cliff top, then descend to the wall.

on_eagle_s_nest_ice.blurb: A winter ice crag in the town of Bancroft, in the Madawaska Valley of eastern Ontario, with eleven climbs that range from beginner ice to hard mixed. Ten are ice and one is mixed, mostly WI2 to WI4+, with a single M5 line in the mix. Most of the lines are set up for top-roping, though a few can be led, and one is a two-pitch gully. Dirty Harry combines ice and rock at WI4+ M4 and is a long-running favourite. The face sits right beside the road, so the walk is almost nonexistent. Whether it forms depends on cold stretches, and the rock above is also used by trad and sport climbers outside the ice season.

on_star_trek_sector.blurb: A busy, long-established section of Calabogie's Main Cliff in eastern Ontario, with routes carrying Star Trek names. Eleven climbs, seven on trad gear and four bolted, cover a lot of ground: a 4th-class chute and an easy 5.6 or two, a 5.8, then a solid block of 5.10s and a pair of 5.12s. The lower grades are classic trad outings, while the 5.10s are the most repeated. The rock is fractured, with a mix of sketchy and slabby ground, and grades can feel inconsistent because older and newer routes were rated differently. A short trail leads from the road, and the wider cliff faces west, so early-season days can run cool.
